## Appendix C Trajectory Case Study: Full-Rank Shadowing from Small Initialization

This section studies robustness along the whole GD path rather than at one critical endpoint. Therefore the clean reference is not a single matrix $M_{0}$ . It is the time-indexed noiseless trajectory

$$ M_{t}^{0}=X_{t}^{0}X_{t}^{0\top}, $$

run from the same initialization as the noisy trajectory

$$ M_{t}^{w}=X_{t}^{w}X_{t}^{w\top}. $$

The trajectory robustness question is

$$ \Delta_{t}=\left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

Throughout this section we focus on the full-rank-to-full-rank regime with $k\leq n$ : for the time window under discussion, both $X_{t}^{0}$ and $X_{t}^{w}$ remain full column rank, so $M_{t}^{0}$ and $M_{t}^{w}$ lie on the rank- $k$ PSD manifold. The role of the normal-curvature ratio is now dynamic. A small $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , defined in (85), together with the local Hessian check below, indicates that the rank- $k$ tangent dynamics around $M_{t}^{w}$ are well conditioned, so measurement noise cannot separate the noisy and noiseless trajectories too much during the next steps.

### C.1 Clean and Noisy GD Paths

Let $N_{0}=0$ and $N_{w}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w$ . Starting from the same small random initialization $X_{0}^{0}=X_{0}^{w}=\alpha G$ , define

$$ \displaystyle X_{t+1}^{\zeta} \displaystyle=\left(I+\eta[H(M_{\star}-M_{t}^{\zeta})+N_{\zeta}]\right)X_{t}^{\zeta}, \displaystyle M_{t}^{\zeta} \displaystyle=X_{t}^{\zeta}(X_{t}^{\zeta})^{\top},\qquad\zeta\in\{0,w\}. $$

The clean recursion is the one studied by Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021), up to normalization constants. In their notation the target is $M_{\star}=X_{\star}X_{\star}^{\top}$ , the factor condition number is

$$ \kappa_{X}=\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})}{\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})}}, $$

the search width is $k>r_{\star}$ , $X_{0}=\alpha G$ with entries of $G$ distributed as $N(0,1/\sqrt{k})$ , and the step size satisfies $\eta\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-4}\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{-2}$ . Equivalently, if $\kappa_{M}=\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})/\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})$ , then the step size is of order $\kappa_{M}^{-2}\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})^{-1}$ . Their Theorem 3.3 assumes $k>r_{\star}$ , splits into the regimes $k\geq 2r_{\star}$ and $r_{\star}<k<2r_{\star}$ , and requires rank- $(2r_{\star}+1)$ RIP with constant of order at most $1/(\kappa_{X}^{4}\sqrt{r_{\star}})$ , together with explicit small upper bounds on $\alpha$ . It proves a finite-time early-stopped proximity bound for the clean iterates. In the $k\geq 2r_{\star}$ case, the normalized error after the prescribed number of iterations is bounded by a polynomial factor times $(\alpha/\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}})^{21/16}$ . The exactly parameterized case $k=r_{\star}$ is treated separately in their Theorem 3.4.

The clean result is used here as a reference path. The new object is the shadowing error $\Delta_{t}$ between (84) with and without $w$ . No critical-point comparison is needed.

### C.2 Rank- $k$ Rho and a Shadowing Bound

For a full-rank noisy iterate $M_{t}^{w}$ , let $P_{t}^{w}=P_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ . In this section

$$ G_{w}(M)=H(M-M_{\star})-N_{w} $$

is the noisy matrix gradient. Define

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert\bigl[P_{t}^{w,\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P_{t}^{w,\perp}\bigr]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})}, \displaystyle\mu_{t}^{\rho} \displaystyle=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}. $$

This is the same full-rank denominator as in the endpoint perturbation theorem, but now it is evaluated along the noisy trajectory. The following deterministic shadowing lemma is the trajectory analogue of the endpoint bound. Because trajectory points are not critical points, $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ should be read as a pointwise lower-margin estimate for the local linearized rank- $k$ map, not as an automatic theorem about every GD step.

To make the bridge explicit, let

$$ \Psi_{t}^{0}(M)=\mathcal{R}_{M}\!\left(-\eta\,\grad_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{0}(M)\right) $$

be the noiseless rank- $k$ manifold step in a local chart, with any smooth first-order retraction $\mathcal{R}$ . A sufficient check for the contraction used below is for every $\eta_{M}\in T_{M_{t}^{w}}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\eta_{M},\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{0}(M_{t}^{w})[\eta_{M}]\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq\mu_{t}^{\rho}\left\lVert\eta_{M}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, \displaystyle\eta L_{t} \displaystyle\leq 1. $$

where $L_{t}$ is a local smoothness bound for the charted gradient map. For the local quadratic model, and for the charted map after absorbing higher-order retraction terms into the local check, this gives $\left\lVert D\Psi_{t}^{0}\right\rVert\leq 1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho}$ . Thus the Hessian Rayleigh quotient is the actual trajectory certificate. The ratio (85) is the rank- $k$ normal-block diagnostic that explains when the check should become favorable; at endpoint-critical or tangent-critical points it reduces to the same normal-curvature margin used in Proposition 1.

#### Lemma 8 (Full-rank trajectory shadowing controlled by $\rho$ ).

Fix a time horizon $T$ . Suppose that the paired clean and noisy trajectories remain in a common full-rank $k$ -dimensional chart for $0\leq t\leq T$ . Assume that the local Hessian/smoothness check (86) holds, so the noiseless chart map satisfies

$$ \left\lVert D\Psi_{t}^{0}\right\rVert\leq 1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho}. $$

Then the noisy and noiseless matrix iterates obey

$$ \Delta_{t+1}\leq(1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho})\Delta_{t}+\eta\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, $$

and therefore

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta\prod_{\ell=j+1}^{t-1}(1-\eta\mu_{\ell}^{\rho}). $$

If $\mu_{t}^{\rho}\geq\underline{\mu}>0$ on the whole window and $\eta\underline{\mu}\leq 1$ , then

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left(1-(1-\eta\underline{\mu})^{t}\right)\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

#### Proof.

The only first-order difference between the two local rank- $k$ maps at the same matrix is the tangent projection of $N_{w}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w$ . RIP gives

$$ \left\lVert\Proj_{T_{M_{t}^{w}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}N_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, $$

because tangent matrices have rank at most $2k$ . By assumption, the computed rank- $k$ margin $\mu_{t}^{\rho}=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ certifies the one-step tangent contraction. Combining this contraction of the clean map with the additive noise perturbation gives (87). Iterating the scalar recursion gives (88), and the geometric sum gives (89). ∎

Lemma 8 is the clean trajectory philosophy. The object $M_{t}^{0}$ is the clean iterate at the same time $t$ , not the clean critical endpoint used earlier. The time-varying stability margin is $\mu_{t}^{\rho}=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , where the ratio $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ contains the active floor $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ in its denominator. Early times with a poor rank- $k$ margin contribute large terms to the sum in (88); times with a strong margin damp all previous noise.

### C.3 Stöger–Soltanolkotabi Variables and a $\rho$ -Proxy

The remaining question is how the dynamics make the $\rho$ -margin better or worse. The clean analysis of Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021) introduces a signal/slack split that is useful for interpreting this. Their “noise” term is an internal over-parameterized slack factor, not observation noise $w$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle M_{\star} \displaystyle=V_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}, \displaystyle\qquad P_{\star} \displaystyle=V_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}, \displaystyle\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle=\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star}), \displaystyle\qquad\kappa_{X} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}. $$

For a clean iterate $X_{t}^{0}$ , take the compact SVD

$$ V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}=\widetilde{V}_{t}\Sigma_{t}W_{t}^{\top},\qquad W_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times r_{\star}},\qquad W_{t}^{\top}W_{t}=I, $$

and complete $W_{t}$ to $[W_{t}\ W_{t,\perp}]$ . Following their Section 5.1, write

$$ \displaystyle S_{t} \displaystyle=X_{t}^{0}W_{t},\qquad N_{t}=X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}, \displaystyle X_{t}^{0} \displaystyle=S_{t}W_{t}^{\top}+N_{t}W_{t,\perp}^{\top}. $$

By Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021, Lemma 5.1), the slack factor has column span orthogonal to $V_{\star}$ , and, whenever $V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}$ has full row rank, $S_{t}$ has rank $r_{\star}$ while $N_{t}$ has rank at most $k-r_{\star}$ . Let $V_{S_{t}}$ denote an orthonormal basis for $\operatorname{col}(S_{t})$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle s_{t} \displaystyle=\sigma_{\min}(S_{t}),\quad\nu_{t}=\left\lVert N_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\quad\phi_{t}=\frac{s_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}, \displaystyle\xi_{t} \displaystyle=\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\quad\chi_{t}=\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{s_{t}^{2}}, \displaystyle\varepsilon_{t} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{t}^{0}-M_{\star})\right\rVert_{F}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

The angle $\xi_{t}$ is the clean signal-factor angle; in Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021), Lemma 9.1 grows the projected signal singular value, Lemma 9.2 controls the internal slack factor, and Lemma 9.3 gives the direct angle recurrence. The auxiliary $\varepsilon_{t}$ is used below only to quote their Phase III refinement; it is not a separate term in the four-metric dashboard. With sensing distortion one also uses the top $r_{\star}$ -dimensional spectral space $P_{H}$ of $H(M_{\star})$ and the upper proxy

$$ \theta_{t}=\left\lVert V_{S_{t}}^{\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\qquad\xi_{t}\leq\theta_{t}, $$

where the second term is controlled by Davis–Kahan when $\left\lVert H(M_{\star})-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\ll\lambda_{\star}$ .

The strict full-rank robustness ratio uses the smallest rank- $k$ eigenvalue of the noisy iterate. Normalize this floor by the signal scale:

$$ \psi_{t}^{w}=\frac{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

The normal block is easiest to read through one subspace metric. For the mathematical bound we use the target alignment

$$ m_{t}^{w}=\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

This measures how much of the true signal space is still visible from the noisy normal space. It is small when the noisy rank- $k$ range contains the target signal space. If $P_{\star}$ is unavailable and the spectral surrogate $P_{H}$ is used instead, then

$$ m_{t}^{w}\leq\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}, $$

and the second term is controlled by Davis–Kahan under the spectral closeness condition stated above. The normalized external noise level is

$$ \eta_{w}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

On a bootstrap window where Lemma 8 keeps $\Delta_{t}=O(\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2})$ , the clean/noisy path discrepancy is folded into the same relaxed noise scale. The signal-floor/slack part is represented by the measured floor $\psi_{t}^{w}$ and the slack tail

$$ \tau_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\chi_{t}\phi_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

Thus $\tau_{t}$ is not another signal-growth variable; it is the Frobenius-sized energy of the $k-r_{\star}$ internal slack directions, normalized by the target spectral floor.

The following lemma is the promised mathematical bound. It has two fixed constants, not two new trajectory metrics. The constant $c_{\rm sh}$ says that the noisy and clean paths are already in the small-noise shadowing window, and $c_{\rm sig}$ is the clean signal-block radius. For example, $c_{\rm sig}=5\sqrt{r_{\star}}\kappa_{X}^{2}$ is valid whenever $\left\lVert S_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ , because then

$$ \left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}\leq 5\sqrt{r_{\star}}\,\kappa_{X}^{2}\lambda_{\star}. $$

#### Lemma 9 (Four-metric upper bound for the trajectory $\rho$ ).

Assume $k>r_{\star}$ . Fix a full-rank time $t$ in the trajectory window. Suppose

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{t} \displaystyle=\left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}\leq c_{\rm sh}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, \displaystyle\left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}. $$

Equivalently, the margin in Lemma 8 is positive whenever the numerator in (96) is smaller than $(1-\delta)\psi_{t}^{w}$ . If the surrogate $P_{H}$ is used, replace $(m_{t}^{w})^{2}$ by

$$ \left(\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\right)^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $P=P_{t}^{w}$ and

$$ B=P^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P^{\perp}. $$

Since $\left\lVert[B]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\left\lVert v\right\rVert=1,\ v\in\operatorname{range}(P^{\perp})}[-v^{\top}Bv]_{+}$ , it is enough to bound the negative Rayleigh quotient on a unit normal vector $v$ . Using $M_{t}^{0}=S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}+N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-v^{\top}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})v \displaystyle=-v^{\top}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})v \displaystyle-v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle-v^{\top}H(N_{t}N_{t}^{\top})v \displaystyle+v^{\top}N_{w}v. $$

The shadowing and observation-noise terms satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\Delta_{t} \displaystyle\leq c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\,\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}, \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}N_{w}v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}. $$

For the active signal block, restricted polarization gives

$$ \displaystyle v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle\geq v^{\top}(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle-\delta\left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

This polarization step uses only the unified $2k$ -RIP, because $\rank(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})\leq 2r_{\star}$ and the trajectory case has $k>r_{\star}$ , so $2r_{\star}+1\leq 2k$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\left[-v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v\right]_{+} \displaystyle\leq\left[v^{\top}(M_{\star}-S_{t}S_{t}^{\top})v\right]_{+} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq v^{\top}M_{\star}v+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})\left\lVert P_{\star}v\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\star}\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Finally,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}H(N_{t}N_{t}^{\top})v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\nu_{t}^{2} \displaystyle=(1+\delta)\tau_{t}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Combining these four estimates and dividing by $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})=\psi_{t}^{w}\lambda_{\star}$ gives (96). ∎

Combining Lemmas 8 and 9 gives the explicit trajectory perturbation bound. Define the four-metric upper envelope

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{k,t} \displaystyle=\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}, \displaystyle\bar{\mu}_{t} \displaystyle=(1-\delta)-\bar{\rho}_{k,t}. $$

On any time window where the hypotheses of Lemma 9 hold at each time and the local Hessian check in (86) holds, if $\bar{\mu}_{t}>0$ , then $\mu_{t}^{\rho}\geq\bar{\mu}_{t}$ and

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta\prod_{\ell=j+1}^{t-1}(1-\eta\bar{\mu}_{\ell}). $$

In particular, if $\bar{\mu}_{t}\geq\underline{\mu}>0$ on the window, then

$$ \left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

This is the actual robustness statement in the trajectory section: alignment, slack, noise, and the active floor determine $\bar{\rho}_{k,t}$ , and the gap $\bar{\mu}_{t}=(1-\delta)-\bar{\rho}_{k,t}$ determines the perturbation size. The bootstrap form is non-circular. Fix a desired uniform margin $\underline{\mu}>0$ and set

$$ c_{\rm sh}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}. $$

If, with this predetermined value of $c_{\rm sh}$ , the envelope (97) satisfies

$$ \bar{\rho}_{k,t}\leq 1-\delta-\underline{\mu}\qquad\text{for every }0\leq t\leq T, $$

then (99) gives

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq c_{\rm sh}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\qquad\text{for every }0\leq t\leq T. $$

Thus the shadowing condition used inside Lemma 9 is proved by induction on the same window, rather than assumed after the fact.

The exact ratio $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ remains directly computable from (85). Lemma 9 gives the relaxed four-metric upper bound

$$ \widehat{\rho}_{k,t}^{\rm traj}:=\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+\tau_{t}+\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}. $$

This is the readable version of (96) after folding the fixed RIP-bias term $\delta c_{\rm sig}$ and the fixed shadowing constant $c_{\rm sh}$ into constants. The measured certificate remains $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , but now the section has an explicit upper bound:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle\approx\widehat{\rho}_{k,t}^{\rm traj}. $$

The denominator $\psi_{t}^{w}$ is the active full-rank floor. The middle term is the slack tail created by the extra $k-r_{\star}$ columns. Here “active” means active in the rank- $k$ chart, not necessarily signal-aligned with $M_{\star}$ ; when $k>r_{\star}$ , the floor may be carried by the thinnest retained slack direction. The remaining noise term $\eta_{w}$ absorbs the small perturbation effects we are deliberately not separating in this relaxed dashboard. Even excellent signal variables do not certify strict full-rank robustness if $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ is still microscopic.

To see (100), set $P=P_{t}^{w}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle P^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P^{\perp} \displaystyle=P^{\perp}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})P^{\perp} \displaystyle+P^{\perp}H(M_{t}^{0}-M_{\star})P^{\perp} \displaystyle-P^{\perp}N_{w}P^{\perp}. $$

For a unit vector $v\in\operatorname{range}(P_{t}^{w,\perp})$ , Cauchy–Schwarz and RIP give $\left\lvert v^{\top}N_{w}v\right\rvert\lesssim\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}$ . The clean residual is controlled by the single misalignment metric $m_{t}^{w}$ : larger $m_{t}^{w}$ means the noisy normal space still sees signal directions and can therefore contain more negative normal curvature. The slack block has Frobenius norm at most

$$ \sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\nu_{t}^{2}=\tau_{t}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Dividing the corresponding rigorous estimate by $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})=\psi_{t}^{w}\lambda_{\star}$ is precisely Lemma 9. The simplified display (100) only suppresses the fixed constants from (96); the exact robustness certificate is still the measured $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ together with the Hessian check (86).

### C.4 Clean Phase Dynamics and the Evolution of the $\rho$ -Proxy

The robustness quantity in this section is always the strict full-rank margin $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ from (85). The proxy (100) only explains its moving parts. Once the measured ratio gives a positive margin and the local Hessian check passes, Lemma 8 converts that margin into the shadowing bound (88). The phase story below is therefore a story about the dashboard in (100): how the single misalignment metric $m_{t}^{w}$ , the slack tail $\tau_{t}$ , the noise level $\eta_{w}$ , and the measured rank- $k$ floor $\psi_{t}^{w}$ evolve.

#### Phase I: spectral alignment.

The first phase is controlled by the power-method comparison in Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021, Lemmas 8.1–8.2). They compare GD to the linearized iterate

$$ \widetilde{X}_{t}=(I+\eta H(M_{\star}))^{t}X_{0} $$

and show that $X_{t}^{0}$ remains close to $\widetilde{X}_{t}$ while the iterate is small. Their Lemma 8.3 gives SVD perturbation bounds for the approximate power iterate $Z_{t}X_{0}+E_{t}$ ; Lemma 8.4 translates top-left-singular-space alignment into properties of $X_{t}^{0}W_{t}$ and $X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}$ ; Lemma 8.5 combines these two steps, under spectral closeness $H(M_{\star})=M_{\star}+\widetilde{E}$ , small $\left\lVert\widetilde{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}/\lambda_{\star}$ , and the corresponding small power-method error parameter, into lower bounds on $\sigma_{\min}(X_{t}^{0}W_{t})$ , upper bounds on $\left\lVert X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}\right\rVert$ , and angle bounds for $\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ . Their Theorem 8.8 supplies the Gaussian smallest-singular-value lower bound for an $r_{\star}\times k$ Gaussian matrix with entries normalized by $1/\sqrt{k}$ :

$$ \sigma_{\min}(G)\geq\varepsilon\,\frac{\sqrt{k}-\sqrt{r_{\star}-1}}{\sqrt{k}} $$

with probability at least $1-(C\varepsilon)^{k-r_{\star}+1}-e^{-ck}$ . This is the probabilistic source of improved initial overlap under over-parameterization.

In the dashboard (100), Phase I primarily reduces the clean component of $m_{t}^{w}$ . More precisely, Lemma 8.5 controls the clean subspace angle through $\xi_{t}$ after the approximate power-method phase, while the small-noise/bootstrap condition keeps the noisy component at the $\eta_{w}$ scale. In this relaxed view, Phase I is best viewed as subspace preparation: the trajectory has learned where the signal is, but the full-rank chart may still be fragile.

#### Phase II: saddle avoidance and signal-floor growth.

After alignment, the clean trajectory obeys the signal-floor growth inequality (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemma 9.1)

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t+1}^{0}) \displaystyle\geq\left(1+\frac{1}{4}\eta\lambda_{\star}\right)\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}) \displaystyle-\eta\,\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0})^{3}. $$

under their step-size, angle, norm, and RIP-error conditions. While this projected signal floor is below signal scale, and while $\xi_{t}=\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ remains small, it is comparable to $\sigma_{\min}(S_{t})$ up to the principal-angle factor $\sqrt{1-\xi_{t}^{2}}$ . Hence a useful reading is

$$ s_{t+1}\gtrsim s_{t}(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star}),\qquad\phi_{t+1}\gtrsim\phi_{t}(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star})^{2}. $$

The same analysis controls the slack factor $\nu_{t}=\left\lVert N_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ and the signal angle (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemmas 9.2–9.3). In the proof of Theorem 9.6, starting from a post-spectral time $t_{0}$ with initial signal scale $\gamma$ , Phase II is summarized by inductive bounds of the form

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}) \displaystyle\gtrsim(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star})^{t-t_{0}}\gamma, \displaystyle\nu_{t} \displaystyle\lesssim(1+c_{\rm slack}\eta\lambda_{\star})^{t-t_{0}}\gamma, \displaystyle\xi_{t} \displaystyle\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-2}. $$

Therefore the clean signal floor grows while the slack ratio $\chi_{t}=\nu_{t}^{2}/s_{t}^{2}$ and the angle remain controlled. In the dashboard (100), this is the favorable middle regime: $m_{t}^{w}$ is small because the surrogate signal space is aligned, while $\tau_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\chi_{t}\phi_{t}$ is harmless only if the product $\chi_{t}\phi_{t}$ remains small relative to $\psi_{t}^{w}$ . The noise level $\eta_{w}$ is the fixed floor. The measured denominator $\psi_{t}^{w}$ can become meaningful if the smallest rank- $k$ direction is no longer microscopic. The caveat is the slack tail

$$ (1+\delta)\tau_{t}=(1+\delta)\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

Lemma 9.2 controls slack relative to the signal factor, but the proxy cares about $\tau_{t}/\psi_{t}^{w}$ . Thus slack stays harmless only when its normalized energy remains small relative to the measured rank- $k$ floor. For strict full-rank robustness, the decisive test is still whether the computed

$$ \rho_{k,t}^{-}=\frac{\left\lVert[P_{t}^{w,\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P_{t}^{w,\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})} $$

falls below $1-\delta$ . Phase II is the period in which this can happen: the numerator becomes more signal-aligned, while the denominator becomes acceptable if the smallest retained rank- $k$ direction, possibly a slack direction relative to $M_{\star}$ , has grown enough to make the rank- $k$ chart well conditioned.

#### Phase III: local refinement and slack risk.

Once $s_{t}$ reaches signal scale, the active reconstruction error contracts (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemma 9.5):

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{\star}-M_{t+1}^{0})\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq(1-c\eta\lambda_{\star})\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{\star}-M_{t}^{0})\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle+C\eta\lambda_{\star}\left\lVert N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

Their Theorem 9.6 then combines Phase II and Phase III. Its post-spectral hypotheses include $\min\{k,n\}>r_{\star}$ , bounded iterate norm, small slack, alignment $\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t_{0}}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-2}$ , an initial signal scale

$$ \gamma\leq\frac{c\,\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}{\min\{k,n\}\kappa_{X}^{2}}, $$

and a rank- $(2r_{\star}+1)$ RIP constant of order at most $1/(\kappa_{X}^{4}\sqrt{r_{\star}})$ . Under these hypotheses, the additional iteration count is

$$ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\eta\lambda_{\star}}\log\!\left(\max\left\{1,\frac{\kappa_{X}r_{\star}}{\min\{k,n\}-r_{\star}}\right\}\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert}{\gamma}\right)\right) $$

and the clean error is bounded by a polynomial factor times $(\gamma/\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert)^{21/16}$ . In the dashboard (100), Phase III no longer introduces a separate active-error metric; the four-metric view keeps $\eta_{w}$ as the fixed external noise floor and tracks the remaining risk through $\tau_{t}$ . This is good for clean active reconstruction, but it is not by itself a strict full-rank robustness certificate. The slack tail can still dominate if the extra columns fail to decay relative to $\psi_{t}^{w}$ . Then $\tau_{t}/\psi_{t}^{w}$ can flatten or increase, and the strict full-rank $\rho$ -margin stops improving.

The trajectory-aware stopping rule is therefore simple: continue while the measured $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ decreases or the shadowing bound (88) tightens; stop, damp, or truncate once the full-rank $\rho$ -margin stops improving.
